paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A transform fault, also called a transform boundary, is a fault that runs along a plate boundary and whose motion is mostly horizontal. It is a strike-slip fault of a special kind, one that also forms a plate boundary. Transform boundaries have another name, conservative plate boundaries, because no lithosphere is added or lost at Earth's surface.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are found
paragraphs.text: A transform fault ends abruptly where it joins another plate boundary, which may be a spreading ridge, a subduction zone or another transform. Most transform faults are in oceanic crust. There they take up the sideways offset between segments of divergent boundaries, which makes a zigzag pattern. A smaller number are on land, and these are generally the better-known ones, such as the San Andreas Fault and the North Anatolian Fault.

paragraphs.heading: Seafloor sliding past seafloor
paragraphs.text: Transform faults commonly link segments of mid-oceanic ridges. These ridges are where new seafloor is constantly made as new basaltic magma wells up. As new seafloor is pushed and pulled outward, older seafloor slides slowly away from the ridges, toward the continents. The ridge segments are separated by only tens of kilometers, yet that separation makes portions of the seafloor push past each other in opposing directions. This sideways movement of seafloor past seafloor is where transform faults are currently active.

paragraphs.heading: A surprising direction of slip
paragraphs.text: John Tuzo Wilson, a geophysicist and geologist, recognized that where faults offset oceanic ridges, the offsets do not follow the classical pattern seen in an offset fence or geological marker. Transform faults slip in the opposite direction from what the standard interpretation of an offset feature would suggest. Slip along a transform fault does not widen the gap between the ridges it separates. The ridges stay where they are, in fixed locations, while the new seafloor made at them is pushed away. A study of fault plane solutions confirmed the hypothesis.

paragraphs.heading: Fracture zones
paragraphs.text: Active transform faults lie between two tectonic structures or faults. Fracture zones mark transform-fault lines that used to be active. They have moved past the active transform zone and are now being pushed toward the continents. These raised ridges on the ocean floor can be followed for hundreds of miles, sometimes all the way across an ocean from one continent to the other.

paragraphs.heading: Growing, steady or shrinking
paragraphs.text: A transform fault that links a spreading center to the upper block of a subduction zone will grow in length. In other cases the length stays constant. Between two ridges, both ridges keep growing outward, and that cancels any change in length. In rare cases a transform fault can shrink, which happens when it links two descending subduction plates. As those plates are subducted, the fault gets shorter until it disappears completely, leaving only two subduction zones that face in opposite directions.

paragraphs.heading: Left or right
paragraphs.text: Transform faults can also be classified as sinistral or dextral. Looking down from above, a sinistral fault is one where a block moves left relative to the block opposite. In a dextral fault, a block moves right relative to the block opposite.
